client: I've been really struggling since my mom passed away six months ago. It's like this heavy fog that just won't lift, and the worst part is that everyone around me seems to have just... moved on with their lives, like nothing happened. I came here because I don't know what else to do, but honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — losing your mom, and then feeling almost invisible in your grief while the world keeps moving around you. I want you to know that your doubt about whether talking will help makes complete sense, especially when you're this exhausted and this unsure. I'm glad you came anyway, and I'd really like to understand more about what this fog has felt like for you day to day — would you be willing to share a little more about that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, okay. Day to day it's like... I'll wake up and for just a second everything feels normal, and then it hits me again that she's gone, and it's like the whole day just collapses before it even starts. I've been calling in sick to work more than I should, and I can't seem to make myself do basic things like cook a real meal or answer texts from friends.
therapist: That moment you describe — waking up and having just a second of peace before it all comes crashing back — sounds absolutely exhausting to live through, day after day. As you're telling me this, I notice something that feels almost quieter than the words themselves, like maybe there's even more weight here than you're letting on. Can I ask — when you imagine reaching out to those friends or making yourself a meal, what's the feeling that stops you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, it's this weird mix of guilt and just... what's the point. Like, my mom was the person I would have called when something was wrong, and now that she's the thing that's wrong, there's nobody who would actually get it the way she would have. And reaching out to friends feels almost fake, like I'd just be performing being okay for their benefit rather than actually getting any real comfort.
therapist: What you just described is one of the most painful parts of this kind of loss — your mom wasn't just your mom, she was your person, the one who made sense of everything, and now the very thing you'd need her for is losing her. That image of "performing being okay" for friends really stays with me, because it sounds like you've been holding so much alone, maybe even in this conversation. I'm wondering — is there any part of you that believes you *deserve* to be comforted, even if it can't come from her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That question kind of stops me, honestly. I think part of me feels like I don't deserve it, or maybe more like... I haven't earned it, because I wasn't there enough for her toward the end, I was so caught up in my own life. So when I think about accepting comfort from someone, there's this voice that says I don't get to feel better yet, like I need to suffer through this as some kind of payment.
therapist: That voice telling you that you need to "earn" relief through suffering — that's such a painful thing to carry, and it's also one of the most common ways grief and guilt can twist together into something that keeps you stuck. I want to gently ask: if your mom were here and she knew you were punishing yourself this way, what do you think she would say to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I know she'd tell me to stop being so hard on myself, that she wouldn't want this for me. But that almost makes it worse, because then I feel guilty for even knowing that and still not being able to just... let it go, like I'm failing her in a whole new way by not honoring what she would have wanted. It's like I can't win no matter which direction I turn.
therapist: The way you just said that — it came out quickly, but there was something almost small and exhausted underneath it, like you've been turning this loop over and over until you're worn down to the bone. You've built a trap where healing feels like betrayal, and knowing the way out somehow becomes another reason to feel bad — that's not a character flaw, that's a mind in a tremendous amount of pain trying to make sense of something that doesn't make sense. I'm curious — when you hear yourself describe that trap out loud, what does it feel like to finally put words to it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: It's strange, because putting words to it does feel like something, like a tiny bit of pressure releasing, but then immediately I second-guess whether that's real or if I'm just... performing insight now the same way I'd perform being okay for my friends. I guess I'm scared that understanding the trap isn't the same as getting out of it, and that I'll leave here feeling like I figured something out and then wake up tomorrow and it'll all be just as heavy as before. That's happened to me before, where a moment of clarity just evaporates.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense, and I want to honor it rather than talk you out of it — you're not being cynical, you're being honest about what you've experienced before. What I'd offer is this: the goal here isn't one big moment of clarity that fixes everything, but slowly building small, real things you can return to when the fog rolls back in. That tiny bit of pressure releasing you felt just now — even if it doesn't last, it tells us something important about what might actually help you, and that's worth paying attention to.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that small things can add up, but I also don't really know what those small things would even look like for me right now. Like, everything that used to feel manageable or comforting just reminds me of her, so I don't know where to even start without running into that grief again. It feels like the whole landscape has changed and I don't have a map anymore.
therapist: You're speaking quickly, like there's a lot rushing through you, but underneath that I notice something that sounds almost... quieter, more tired than the words themselves — like part of you has already half-given up on finding that map before you've even started looking. I want to sit with what you said about grief being everywhere, because that's real, but I'm also curious — when you imagine running into that grief in a small moment, is it always only painful, or has there ever been a flicker of something else, like closeness to her, mixed in with it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Actually... yeah, sometimes when I make her recipe for that soup she used to make, I feel close to her for a moment before the sadness takes over. But I almost feel guilty admitting that, like I'm trying to find a silver lining when I should just be letting myself grieve properly, whatever that even means. I don't know if that flicker of closeness is something I'm allowed to lean into or if it's just me avoiding the real pain.
therapist: That soup is not a detour around grief — it *is* grief, and love, and her, all at once, and the fact that you feel close to her in that moment isn't avoidance, it's actually one of the most honest connections you have to her right now. I notice something in how you described it, almost like the words came faster, a little brighter, even as you were trying to talk yourself out of it — like some part of you already knows that flicker matters. What if "grieving properly" isn't about staying only in the pain, but about letting yourself hold both the loss and the love at the same time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That reframe actually lands somewhere real in me, but I'm also a little skeptical, because it sounds almost too clean, like a nice idea that might not hold up when I'm actually in the middle of it. When I'm making that soup and the sadness hits, I'm not sure I have the presence of mind to also hold onto the love part, it just kind of swamps everything else. I guess I'm wondering if that's something you actually learn to do, or if it's just something that sounds right in a therapy room but falls apart at home.
therapist: Your skepticism is actually a really healthy sign — it means you're not just accepting a nice idea, you're asking whether it can survive contact with real pain, and that's exactly the right question. The honest answer is that it is something you learn, not something you just decide, and it starts small — not holding both feelings perfectly in the moment, but maybe just noticing afterward that the closeness was also there, even if the sadness was louder. Would you be open to trying that just once this week — making the soup, letting whatever comes come, and then gently asking yourself afterward if any trace of her felt present in a way that wasn't only painful?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think I could maybe try that, but I'm already anticipating that I'll either avoid making the soup altogether because it feels like too much, or I'll make it and just get swamped by the sadness and forget to do the noticing part afterward. It's like I can see myself failing the homework before I've even started it, which I know probably sounds defeatist. I guess I'm asking, what do I do if I try and it just hurts and there's nothing else there?
therapist: First, I want to say that anticipating the ways something might go wrong isn't defeatism — it's actually your mind trying to protect you, and we can work with that rather than against it. If you make the soup and it just hurts and there's nothing else there, that's not failure — that's still you showing up for yourself, and the pain itself is information, not proof that you're broken or that healing isn't possible. What if we agreed that the only way to "fail" this week is not to be kind to yourself afterward, whatever happens?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
